title: No inventory of AI tools in use
summary: No record exists of which AI systems, models, agents, or AI-backed SaaS features are operating in the environment, by whom, or against which data.

cloud_agnostic.summary: Stand up a single AI asset register before tooling. Four columns is enough at this stage: tool name, data classification accessed, human owner, approved or not. Front any sanctioned LLM calls through a logging gateway so usage is at least observable. LiteLLM and Open WebUI are the common OSS starting points; both can sit between users/apps and any model provider.

aws_bedrock.summary: Stand up the inventory across two AWS surfaces. For managed services: enable Bedrock model invocation logging to CloudWatch and capture model access via CloudTrail data events. For shadow agents and SaaS-installed assistants: use IAM Access Analyzer and AWS Config conformance packs to catch unexpected Bedrock identities.

title: No understanding of AI-specific threats
summary: The security team cannot describe what prompt injection, data exfiltration via model output, model inversion, training-data poisoning, or model extraction look like in the organization's environment.

cloud_agnostic.summary: Read the OWASP AI Exchange threat sections (2 through 4) and the MITRE ATLAS matrix together. Both are vendor-neutral and free. For hands-on practice, run Garak against any LLM you can hit, including hosted endpoints.

aws_bedrock.summary: Use the AWS Generative AI Security Scoping Matrix as the starting threat-awareness reference; it categorizes AI risks by deployment pattern (consumer SaaS, enterprise SaaS, foundation model, customized model, self-trained).

links.label: AWS Generative AI Security Scoping Matrix

title: Any internal AI/ML models are unprotected
summary: Internal models, training data, and inference endpoints have no access controls, monitoring, or threat modeling beyond whatever the underlying compute happens to provide.

cloud_agnostic.summary: If you have any internal models or fine-tunes, treat them like production code: store weights in artifact storage with access logging, never serve directly from a developer workstation, put inference behind an authenticated proxy, and tag every endpoint as Confidential or Internal in the asset register.

aws_bedrock.summary: Custom models live in SageMaker. Put them in a private VPC, attach a SageMaker Model Registry with approval gating, and front inference endpoints with VPC endpoints rather than public URLs.

title: No visibility into the AI supply chain
summary: Models, datasets, and AI-enabled libraries enter the environment without provenance, signature verification, or vendor risk review.

cloud_agnostic.summary: Treat models like dependencies. Pin model identifiers, capture a hash, and require a documented source URL for every model entering the environment. ModelScan and picklescan catch the most common pickle-format risks in Hugging Face artifacts.

aws_bedrock.summary: Prefer Bedrock Marketplace and SageMaker JumpStart for third-party models; both record source, license, and version in account-scoped registries. Block direct downloads from public model hubs at the VPC egress proxy.

title: Developers pulling models from Hugging Face or similar repositories without verification
summary: Engineers download pretrained weights ad hoc, often in pickle formats, with no verification step. Pickle files can execute arbitrary code on load.

cloud_agnostic.summary: Prefer safetensors over pickle. Scan any pickle artifact before load. Mirror approved models into an internal registry so downloads do not happen at run time from arbitrary external hosts.

links.label: MITRE ATLAS: ML Supply Chain Compromise

aws_bedrock.summary: Use JumpStart or Marketplace as the canonical model source. If a use case demands a Hugging Face model not in JumpStart, mirror through a controlled S3 bucket after pickle-scanning; never let SageMaker training jobs download from public hubs at run time.

title: No visibility into third-party AI agents or plugins granted access to corporate environments
summary: OAuth-installed agents, browser extensions, and AI-augmented SaaS plugins reach corporate data without an inventory or access review.

cloud_agnostic.summary: Pull OAuth grant logs from your identity provider and list every third-party app with read access to mail, docs, or chat. Revoke anything that no owner can name. Repeat monthly until BYOAI surface is bounded.

links.label: OWASP Top 10 for LLM Apps (LLM06: Excessive Agency)

aws_bedrock.summary: Audit IAM identities with `bedrock:InvokeModel` or `bedrock-agent:*` through IAM Access Analyzer. Any identity outside the AI inventory is a candidate for removal or onboarding.

title: No AI/ML used in security tools or operations
summary: Detection, triage, and response are entirely rules-based or human-driven. Vendor AI features in existing tools are either absent or disabled.

cloud_agnostic.summary: Audit the SIEM/EDR/SOAR you already pay for. Vendor-shipped ML detections (UEBA modules, anomaly baselines) are the cheapest first step. Enable them at vendor defaults, document the change, and reassess in 30 days.

aws_bedrock.summary: Turn on the AWS security services that already ship ML detections: GuardDuty (with all data sources enabled), Macie, and Inspector. Pipe Security Hub findings into a single review.

title: The security team is unaware of available AI capabilities
summary: Security engineers cannot describe what AI features their existing tools ship with, what they cost, or what they would change if enabled.

cloud_agnostic.summary: Have each tool owner produce a one-page brief on the AI features in their product, default state (on/off), tier dependency, and known false-positive behavior. Compile into an internal index.

aws_bedrock.summary: AWS Skill Builder has a free generative AI learning plan and a paid security path. Set a baseline expectation that at least one engineer per security domain completes it.

title: Manual processes dominate detection and response
summary: Alerts are triaged by hand, with no automated enrichment, no model-assisted classification, and no playbook automation.

cloud_agnostic.summary: Capture the top 10 alerts by volume and time-to-disposition. Anything routine and high-volume is a candidate for automation before AI: SOAR-style playbooks first, model-assisted triage later when there is baseline data to evaluate it against.

aws_bedrock.summary: Wire EventBridge rules off Security Hub findings into Step Functions or Lambda for automated triage of routine alert classes (e.g., GuardDuty IAM finding categories).

title: No AI usage policy exists
summary: There is no written policy stating which AI tools are permitted, what data can be entered, or who owns AI decisions.

cloud_agnostic.summary: Draft a one-page AI acceptable use policy in week one. State sanctioned tools, prohibited tools, what data classes can be entered into each, the policy owner, and the consequence model. Publish it, attest it, and revisit in 90 days. Policy precision improves with usage data; do not block on perfection.

aws_bedrock.summary: Add an SCP at the organization root that denies all `bedrock:*` actions outside designated accounts. That forces every AI use case to ride through an approved account where logging and policy apply.

title: BYOAI proliferates unchecked
summary: Employees use personal or unapproved AI tools (ChatGPT, Claude.ai, Gemini, niche assistants) for work tasks. There is no policy to call this Shadow AI; it is BYOAI.

cloud_agnostic.summary: Run a BYOAI discovery survey before blocking. Anonymous, opt-in, listing tools and use cases. Pair with egress log review for known AI domains. The output is a sanctioned list and a remediation list; not a punishment list.

aws_bedrock.summary: An SCP that allows `bedrock:InvokeModel` only for approved model IDs is the structural enforcement; pair with a Bedrock model-invocation logging policy so even allowed use is observable.

title: No visibility into what AI tools employees are using
summary: There is no log of AI domain access, no DLP rule for AI endpoints, and no integration between identity and AI usage.

cloud_agnostic.summary: Start with egress logs. Most networks see AI tool access concentrated in a small set of domains. A weekly report of top AI domains by user (or by department) is enough to start governing. CASB or SASE products extend this with policy at the proxy.

aws_bedrock.summary: VPC Flow Logs plus a curated AI-domain enrichment list in your SIEM gives department-level visibility into external AI tool usage. For Bedrock-internal traffic, model invocation logs cover the same need.

title: No AI risk assessment has been conducted
summary: AI risk is not on the enterprise risk register, is not scored, and is not reviewed in any cadence.

cloud_agnostic.summary: Use the OWASP AI Exchange risk-analysis decision tree as the starting framework. Add a single AI line to the enterprise risk register naming the top three threats your organization plausibly faces (almost certainly: data exfiltration, vendor lock-in or outage, regulatory exposure).

aws_bedrock.summary: AWS Audit Manager has a Generative AI Best Practices framework that exposes a starting set of controls and evidence collectors. The framework alone is not a risk assessment, but it makes the gaps explicit.

title: Leadership unaware of AI exposure
summary: Executives cannot answer 'how much of our data has been sent to public AI models in the last quarter?' or 'who owns AI decisions here?'

cloud_agnostic.summary: Brief leadership with two numbers and one named owner: number of AI tools in the inventory, percentage of staff who have touched one in the last 30 days (egress log estimate is fine), and the named AI governance lead. The point of the brief is to anchor accountability, not to recommend tooling.

aws_bedrock.summary: Cost Explorer tagged by service surfaces Bedrock and SageMaker spend trend lines that translate well to executive briefs. Pair with a count of distinct IAM identities invoking Bedrock per month.

title: No distinction is made between conversational AI and action-taking AI
summary: Policy and threat modeling treat chatbots and agentic systems identically, ignoring that agents can invoke functions, send mail, write code, and authorize transactions.

cloud_agnostic.summary: Add a single sentence to the policy: 'AI that can take actions on systems requires explicit security review before deployment, separate from conversational AI.' That sentence does most of the work at Stage 1. Implementation comes at Stage 3.

links.label: OWASP Agentic AI Threats and Mitigations

aws_bedrock.summary: Bedrock distinguishes model invocation (InvokeModel) from agentic action (Agents for Bedrock and AgentCore). Treat any role with `bedrock-agent:*` permissions as agentic in your policy.

title: Inventory of sanctioned AI tools exists but may be incomplete
summary: A list of approved AI tools is maintained but rarely reconciled against actual usage. Shadow AI is suspected but unmeasured.

cloud_agnostic.summary: Reconcile the inventory against actual egress quarterly. Anything in egress but not in the inventory is either an addition or a remediation. Use Phin, Hatching, or just SIEM correlations against a curated AI-domain list.

aws_bedrock.summary: AWS Config conformance packs against Bedrock and SageMaker resources reconcile the inventory automatically. Drift becomes a Security Hub finding.

title: Basic understanding of AI risks at the leadership level
summary: Leadership recognizes AI as a risk category but does not yet have a defended risk taxonomy or assigned risk owners.

cloud_agnostic.summary: Adopt a five-risk taxonomy and stop there for now: data leakage, model misuse, third-party AI, regulatory, hallucination/legal. Anything more granular is overkill at Stage 2.

title: No AI-specific security testing
summary: Existing pentests do not include prompt injection, model extraction, or instruction-manipulation cases. AI components are in scope only by accident.

cloud_agnostic.summary: Add an AI testing rider to the next pentest scope. At minimum: prompt injection (direct and indirect), output handling for PII, and basic model extraction prompts. Garak and Promptfoo cover most of this in OSS.

aws_bedrock.summary: Bedrock model evaluation supports automated and human evaluation jobs against curated test sets, including custom adversarial sets seeded by Garak or Promptfoo output.

title: Basic visibility into where models originate
summary: Engineering can describe where the models in use came from (vendor, Hugging Face org, internal build), but provenance is not verified cryptographically or tracked in a registry.

cloud_agnostic.summary: Adopt an internal model registry (MLflow, ZenML, or a folder in object storage with hashes and a README). Record source URL, hash, license, and approver.

aws_bedrock.summary: JumpStart model cards and Marketplace listing pages record source, license, training data attestation, and version. Pin to model ARNs in code rather than friendly names.

title: Awareness that pickled model files pose risk
summary: Engineers know pickle deserialization is dangerous but verification is ad hoc.

cloud_agnostic.summary: Mandate safetensors for new internal artifacts. Quarantine any pickle that has not been scanned by ModelScan or picklescan.

aws_bedrock.summary: Bedrock foundation models do not load customer-supplied pickle artifacts. For SageMaker custom training, restrict input sources to S3 buckets owned by the workload account and pickle-scan as part of the data pipeline.

title: Basic awareness of the risks of granting AI tools API access or system integrations
summary: The organization knows that granting a chatbot or assistant API tokens carries risk, but there is no review process before grants are issued.

cloud_agnostic.summary: Require a short threat-model exercise on any AI tool that requests scopes broader than read-only. Add the integration to the asset register before any grant is approved.

aws_bedrock.summary: Treat any AWS principal granted `bedrock-agent:*`, `lambda:InvokeFunction` across boundaries, or cross-account assume-role into an AI workload as an agentic integration requiring threat-model review.

title: Security tools with AI-based features used but not intentionally configured
summary: AI features in the SIEM/EDR are turned on but no one has tuned thresholds, evaluated detections against environment data, or measured false-positive rates.

cloud_agnostic.summary: Pick one AI feature per tool. Document baseline false-positive rate over a fixed window. Tune. Repeat.

aws_bedrock.summary: GuardDuty, Inspector, and Security Hub all ship measurable detection sets. Tune each in a documented sequence, measuring suppression vs. additional findings against a labeled month of incident data.

title: No customization or tuning of AI security features
summary: Detections, summarizations, and alert classifications all run at vendor defaults regardless of environment fit.

cloud_agnostic.summary: Allocate analyst time for tuning. Vendor defaults assume a generic environment; an unconfigured AI feature is usually noisier than its predecessor rule-based detection.

title: Basic spam/malware detection using vendor AI
summary: Mail and endpoint vendors apply their own AI models to detection, but the organization does not contribute telemetry back or evaluate the outcome.

cloud_agnostic.summary: Capture monthly detection rates from each vendor with AI-backed detection. Build a single internal dashboard that compares.

aws_bedrock.summary: GuardDuty Malware Protection plus Amazon SES email feedback metrics give a measurable baseline. Pipe both into a single Security Hub dashboard.

title: No AI strategy for security operations
summary: There is no roadmap for where AI augmentation should land in the SOC workflow.

cloud_agnostic.summary: Pick one workflow (alert triage, IR write-up generation, threat intel summarization) and target it for Stage 3 enablement. Do not try to AI-augment the whole SOC at once.

aws_bedrock.summary: Security Hub's posture management gives a coverage map to plan against. Pick one workflow and target a Bedrock-backed automation (alert summarization or playbook explanation) as the first integration.

title: Security team lacks AI/ML skills
summary: No team member has hands-on experience with prompt engineering, model evaluation, or ML pipeline security.

cloud_agnostic.summary: Send at least one engineer through SANS SEC545 or equivalent. Cross-train so AI security knowledge does not concentrate in a single person.

title: No validation of vendor AI claims
summary: Vendors marketing 'AI-powered' features are accepted at face value. There is no test against environment data or measured outcome.

cloud_agnostic.summary: Add a short AI questionnaire to vendor reviews: what model, on whose data, with what evaluation, under what retention. Refuse procurement of 'AI' features that cannot answer.

aws_bedrock.summary: Bedrock Marketplace and JumpStart listings include the model card, license, and benchmark scores when available. Treat that as the bar for any AI vendor: if they cannot match Marketplace metadata, refuse procurement.

title: AI acceptable use policy published; may be binary rather than nuanced
summary: An AUP exists. Common shape: a list of allowed tools, a list of prohibited tools, and a paragraph on data classes.

cloud_agnostic.summary: Annual policy review with a feedback channel. The Stage 2 policy will be wrong; the only way to improve it is to make it easy to challenge.

aws_bedrock.summary: Encode the policy in SCPs and IAM tag-based conditions. The policy text is the human-readable layer; the SCP is the enforcement layer that prevents drift between intent and reality.

title: Data classification for AI usage is absent or incomplete
summary: The AUP references data classes but the underlying data classification work has not been done or is partial.

cloud_agnostic.summary: Data classification is the Stage 3 prerequisite. If it is not done, this is the next thing to fund. Use Presidio for PII detection in unstructured stores.

aws_bedrock.summary: Macie auto-classifies S3 objects against managed and custom data identifiers. Run a one-shot scan over the data lake to surface PHI / PII / financial data before drafting the AI data classification rules.

title: Basic awareness training mentions AI risks
summary: AI is referenced in annual security training but not addressed in role-specific depth.

cloud_agnostic.summary: Add a five-minute module: what to never paste into AI tools, what to do if you find an AI feature in a vendor product, where to report.

title: No AI risk register
summary: AI risks are not tracked alongside other enterprise risks with owners, treatments, and review cadence.

cloud_agnostic.summary: Add an 'AI' risk category to the existing enterprise risk register. Three to five risks at this stage. Owner, current treatment, residual rating, review date.

aws_bedrock.summary: Use AWS Audit Manager's Generative AI Best Practices framework as the seed for the register; its assessments map to common control families (CC, AC, AT) and emit evidence artifacts.

title: No cross-functional AI governance body
summary: AI decisions are made in silos: legal in one channel, engineering in another, security in a third.

cloud_agnostic.summary: Form a working group, not a committee. Standing 30-minute monthly meeting, named members from security, legal, engineering, and a business sponsor. Output is a public decisions log.

title: Policy begins to differentiate between conversational AI and AI granted permission to take actions
summary: The AUP distinguishes chat-style AI from agentic AI in scope and review requirements.

cloud_agnostic.summary: Define 'agentic AI' in the policy: any AI that invokes tools, writes to systems, or sends communications. Require a security architecture review before any agentic deployment.

aws_bedrock.summary: In AWS terms: `bedrock:InvokeModel` is conversational, `bedrock-agent:*` and AgentCore are agentic. Write the policy with these IAM action families as the dividing line so enforcement is structural, not narrative.

title: Complete inventory of AI systems and models; AI included in asset classification
summary: Every AI system, model, agent, and AI-augmented SaaS feature is recorded with owner, classification, approved use, and review cadence.

cloud_agnostic.summary: Promote the asset register to a system of record with API access for SIEM/SOAR. Reconcile automatically against egress logs and IdP grants.

aws_bedrock.summary: AWS Config recorder for Bedrock, SageMaker, and Lambda resources, with custom rules for AI-specific attributes (model used, knowledge base attached, agent role). Findings to Security Hub.

title: Data flows to and from AI systems are documented with data lineage visibility
summary: For each AI system, the data classes consumed, generated, and persisted are documented end to end.

cloud_agnostic.summary: Use OpenLineage or a comparable lineage tool for ETL into model contexts. Capture system prompt, tool definitions, retrieval index, and output sink.

aws_bedrock.summary: Use AWS DataZone or a SageMaker Feature Store catalog for upstream data lineage. For Bedrock Knowledge Bases, the data source manifest plus CloudTrail data events give end-to-end retrieval lineage.

title: Internal AI agents assigned distinct NHIs with strict access control
summary: Every AI agent has its own Non-Human Identity with scoped credentials, a documented human owner, and least-privilege access to tools, data, and APIs.

cloud_agnostic.summary: Issue short-lived credentials per agent via Vault or SPIFFE. Scope each agent to a single tool surface. Every credential ties back to a named human owner in the asset register.

aws_bedrock.summary: AgentCore Identity issues per-agent IAM roles scoped to `bedrock:InvokeModel` on specific model ARNs and to the exact tool ARNs each agent needs. Tie the role tag to a human-owner attribute enforced by SCP.

title: AI tool and API access strictly scoped
summary: AI tool access is scoped to specific resources, time windows, and operations. No broad credentials.

cloud_agnostic.summary: Define a tool-access policy DSL (OPA, Cedar) that scopes per-agent invocations. Deny by default; allow per tool, per resource.

aws_bedrock.summary: IAM condition keys (`aws:RequestTag`, `bedrock:ModelId`, `bedrock:GuardrailIdentifier`) narrow Invoke permissions to specific models, with guardrails, and for tagged callers.

title: Prompt injection and instruction manipulation defenses implemented
summary: Production AI systems apply layered defenses: input segregation, instruction hierarchy, retrieval sanitization, and output validation.

cloud_agnostic.summary: Combine LLM Guard or NeMo Guardrails for I/O filtering with a system-prompt design that places untrusted content in a clearly demarcated section. Test with Garak and Promptfoo in CI.

aws_bedrock.summary: Bedrock Guardrails apply content filtering, denied topics, contextual grounding checks, and PII redaction inline at InvokeModel time. Combine with prompt-template hygiene that segregates retrieval context.

title: Input validation and output filtering deployed
summary: User-facing AI applications validate inputs against schema and filter outputs for PII, sensitive markers, and unsafe content.

cloud_agnostic.summary: LLM Guard or Promptfoo's redactor for outputs. Presidio for PII. Block-on-confidence rather than allow-on-pass.

aws_bedrock.summary: Bedrock Guardrails for inline filtering, plus Macie scanning of any data the model has read or written to S3. PII redaction settings on the guardrail are scoped per use case.

title: AI systems included in penetration testing scope; basic adversarial emulation conducted
summary: AI systems are scoped into routine pentests with named adversarial test cases.

cloud_agnostic.summary: Add ATLAS-aligned test cases to the pentest SOW. Require evidence of prompt-injection, model-extraction, and instruction-manipulation attempts in the report.

aws_bedrock.summary: AWS customer support policy allows testing of customer-owned AI workloads on Bedrock without prior approval; bring the ATLAS-aligned test cases and supply prompt-injection seeds. Bedrock Guardrails will return blocked-content metadata that helps measure defense efficacy.

title: Model provenance verification in place
summary: Every model entering the environment is verified against its publisher signature or hash before deployment.

cloud_agnostic.summary: Mirror approved models internally with signed manifests. Sigstore for signing. Block direct download from external registries at the egress proxy.

aws_bedrock.summary: JumpStart and Bedrock Marketplace models are signed by AWS or the model publisher and pinned by ARN. Custom models trained via SageMaker can be registered with model approval status and lineage in the registry.

title: Controls mapped to MITRE ATLAS techniques
summary: Defensive controls are inventoried and mapped to the ATLAS techniques they address, exposing coverage gaps.

cloud_agnostic.summary: Reuse the same MITRE ATT&CK Navigator approach you already use for endpoint coverage. ATLAS Navigator JSON is published.

title: Runtime validation of dynamically loaded agent tools and plugins
summary: Agent tool definitions, descriptions, and capabilities are validated at load time against an allow-list of approved tool signatures.

cloud_agnostic.summary: Hash each registered tool definition. Refuse to load a tool whose signature has changed since approval. Audit changes through code review, not at run time.

title: Secure agent-to-agent communication and mutual authentication
summary: Agents authenticate to each other with mTLS or workload identity; messages are bound to identities, not trust-by-default channels.

cloud_agnostic.summary: Service mesh with mTLS (Linkerd, Istio) or SPIFFE SVIDs for direct agent-to-agent calls. Apply OPA policy at the receiving side.

aws_bedrock.summary: Use AgentCore for managed inter-agent communication. For self-hosted agents on ECS or EKS, App Mesh or VPC Lattice with TLS plus IAM auth provides equivalent mutual authentication.

title: AI-powered threat detection tuned to the environment
summary: AI-based detections are tuned against organizational data, with measured precision and recall.

cloud_agnostic.summary: Tune each detection against historical incident data. Capture precision/recall on a labeled subset before promoting a detection to production.

aws_bedrock.summary: GuardDuty and Security Hub provide tunable detection thresholds. SageMaker custom models trained on local detection data integrate via Lambda detectors that emit Security Hub findings.

title: AI-assisted alert triage and prioritization in place
summary: An AI layer triages incoming alerts: deduplication, severity ranking, and recommended next action.

cloud_agnostic.summary: If vendor SOAR ships AI triage, enable and measure it. Where it does not, a small LLM front-end against alert payloads (with redaction) can do the same job for routine alert classes.

aws_bedrock.summary: Lambda-based alert summarization using Bedrock InvokeModel with a guardrail that redacts PII before model invocation. Output back into Security Hub as a note.

title: Behavioral analytics (UEBA) deployed and customized for anomaly detection
summary: UEBA models cover users, service accounts, and AI agent NHIs.

cloud_agnostic.summary: Extend UEBA models to include AI agent NHIs as a distinct identity class with their own baselines.

aws_bedrock.summary: GuardDuty IAM finding types behave as UEBA for AWS principals. Add a custom detection layer for Bedrock invocation patterns: model, region, prompt-size distributions per IAM role.

title: AI-assisted automated playbooks deployed for common scenarios
summary: Routine response actions (phishing reports, suspect IP triage) are partially or fully automated with AI assistance.

cloud_agnostic.summary: Adopt or extend an OSS SOAR (Shuffle, TheHive Cortex). Pair AI summarization with deterministic action steps; never let an LLM be the sole decider on a containment action at this stage.

aws_bedrock.summary: Step Functions orchestrates the deterministic steps; Bedrock InvokeModel as a Lambda task handles the language work (write-ups, classification). Never let Bedrock be the sole decider on a containment branch.

title: AI-powered threat intelligence enrichment
summary: Incoming threat intel is automatically enriched (entity extraction, related-actor mapping, summarization).

cloud_agnostic.summary: Run intel through an LLM with extraction prompts (entities, TTPs, IOCs) and post structured output back into the TIP.

aws_bedrock.summary: Bedrock with a structured-output guardrail for entity / TTP / IOC extraction. Inferentia or Trainium instances handle high-volume enrichment more cost-effectively than on-demand model pricing.

title: Security team trained on AI/ML fundamentals
summary: Engineers understand model evaluation basics, prompt engineering, and AI failure modes.

cloud_agnostic.summary: Adopt a role-based training matrix: general workforce (15 min), engineers (2 hours), AI specialists (multi-day).

aws_bedrock.summary: AWS Skill Builder ML and security learning plans plus the AWS Generative AI Security Scoping Matrix as the org-internal reference. Annual recertification on the matrix.

title: Genuine AI/ML capability and environment compatibility assessed at procurement
summary: Vendors selling AI features must demonstrate genuine capability and fit; AI-washing is rejected.

cloud_agnostic.summary: Require model cards, adversarial test results, and a defined evaluation set from any AI vendor. No proof, no procurement.

aws_bedrock.summary: Marketplace and JumpStart listings include model cards; treat their structure as the bar for non-AWS vendors. No model card, no procurement.

title: AI Governance Council established with cross-functional membership and decision authority
summary: A standing body with security, legal, privacy, engineering, and business representation makes binding decisions on AI use cases.

cloud_agnostic.summary: Publish the charter. Publish decisions. Republish quarterly.

title: Comprehensive AI policy addressing use cases and data classification
summary: Policy is specific by use case and by data class, not binary block/allow.

cloud_agnostic.summary: Map approved tools to data classes in a single table. The policy reads in seconds.

aws_bedrock.summary: Map the policy table to IAM permission boundaries and tag-condition policies; the human-readable policy and the SCP set should be reconciled monthly.

title: AI ethics guidelines established
summary: Ethical considerations (fairness, transparency, human oversight) are codified.

cloud_agnostic.summary: Use NIST AI RMF Playbook prompts to seed the ethics guidelines rather than writing from scratch.

title: Third-party AI assessment requirements defined
summary: Vendor AI systems are assessed against a defined questionnaire before purchase.

cloud_agnostic.summary: Adopt a standard vendor AI questionnaire (HiTRUST AI Risk Management, NIST AI 100-1 derived). Refuse to onboard vendors that decline.

aws_bedrock.summary: Marketplace vendor profiles publish model cards, eval results, and provenance. Build the in-house questionnaire to mirror Marketplace metadata so internal evaluation aligns with the canonical source.

title: AI risks included in the enterprise risk register with a defined assessment methodology
summary: AI risks use a documented method (likelihood, impact, treatment) consistent with the rest of the register.

cloud_agnostic.summary: FAIR (Factor Analysis of Information Risk) extended for AI scenarios is the most common starting point at Stage 3 to 4.

aws_bedrock.summary: Audit Manager assessments emit structured evidence that feeds a FAIR-extended methodology cleanly. Use the Generative AI framework as the starting assessment set and add custom controls per AI scenario.

title: AI-specific incident response procedures in place
summary: IR playbooks address prompt injection, model exfiltration, agent misuse, and AI vendor outages.

cloud_agnostic.summary: Add 'AI incident' as a category in the IR runbook with sub-types: prompt injection, agent misuse, data exfiltration via output, model unavailability.

aws_bedrock.summary: Add Bedrock-specific runbooks: prompt-injection containment (rotate the guardrail and the agent role), data exfiltration via output (revoke Bedrock invoke for the offending role, capture invocation logs for the window), agent misuse (decommission the AgentCore identity).

title: Human-in-the-loop thresholds and automated policy enforcement defined for high-risk agent workflows
summary: Policy decision points, intent gates, and consequence-based checks are defined for high-risk agentic actions.

cloud_agnostic.summary: Codify a 'consequence ladder': low-impact actions can run autonomously, mid-impact require log review, high-impact require synchronous human approval.

aws_bedrock.summary: Step Functions has a wait-for-human-task pattern; AgentCore supports action policies that require explicit approval. Define the consequence ladder once and reference it from both.

title: Every deployed AI agent has a documented human owner
summary: No anonymous agents; every running agent ties to a named human.

cloud_agnostic.summary: The asset register's 'owner' column is the source of truth. Any agent without an owner is decommissioned.

aws_bedrock.summary: Enforce a required tag (Owner=<human-IAM-Identity-Center-user>) on every AgentCore identity via SCP. AWS Config rule flags identities missing the tag for decommission.

title: Structured logging with trace IDs across agent steps and tool calls
summary: Every agent action carries a trace ID that links back to the originating request, system prompt, tool invocation, and result.

cloud_agnostic.summary: Langfuse, Arize Phoenix, or OpenTelemetry GenAI semantic conventions cover this.

aws_bedrock.summary: Bedrock model invocation logging captures request, response, and guardrail decision; AgentCore traces capture each tool step. Stream both to CloudWatch Logs with a per-trace correlation ID; export to S3 for long retention.

title: Security integrated into the AI/ML development lifecycle
summary: Security gates exist at each phase of the AI lifecycle: design, data, training, eval, deploy, monitor.

cloud_agnostic.summary: Define gate criteria per phase. Tie to the standard SDLC change-management workflow.

aws_bedrock.summary: SageMaker Pipelines with Model Cards, Model Monitor, and Clarify covers the end-to-end lifecycle. Promote each pipeline stage to a Security Hub control so gate evidence is centralized.

title: Threat modeling required for all AI systems
summary: STRIDE or PASTA threat models extended for AI threats are mandatory before deployment.

cloud_agnostic.summary: Use the OWASP AI Exchange threat tree as the AI-specific extension to whatever threat-modeling method the org already uses.

title: Confused Deputy defenses deployed to isolate untrusted inputs from agent execution tools
summary: An agent's authority to invoke tools is bound to the request context, not the agent itself, preventing untrusted user inputs from inducing high-authority actions.

cloud_agnostic.summary: Use OPA or Cedar at the tool boundary with the request principal in the policy, not just the agent identity.

aws_bedrock.summary: Add a Lambda authorizer to the AgentCore tool path that re-evaluates the request principal, not just the agent role. AgentCore action policies can carry the consequence ladder as policy attributes.
